30 A diffraction grating has 4.00  105 lines per metre. A beam of light of wavelength 589  10–9
m is
incident normally on the diffraction grating.
What is the angle between the second-order maximum and the direction of the incident beam of
light?
A
13.6
B
27.3
C
28.1
D
56.2

hints: Start from the grating specification $4.00 \times 10^5$ lines per metre and write the slit spacing as $d = 1/N$ in metres.
Recall the normal-incidence grating condition $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ and identify $n = 2$ and $\lambda = 589 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$ for this second-order maximum.
Calculate $\sin\theta = 2\lambda/d$ first, check it is less than 1, then use $\theta = \sin^{-1}(2\lambda/d)$ to find the angle from the zero-order incident direction.
walkthrough: Identify the data: $N = 4.00 \times 10^5 \text{ m}^{-1}$, $\lambda = 589 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$, order $n = 2$, and normal incidence so $\theta$ is measured from the incident beam direction.
State the diffraction grating rule for a maximum: $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$, so $\sin\theta = n\lambda/d$.
Take the inverse sine: $\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.4712) = 28.1^{\circ}$, with the same degree unit as the options.

A.explanation: This is the first-order angle with $n = 1$, since $\sin\theta = 589 \times 10^{-9} / 2.50 \times 10^{-6}$ gives $13.6^{\circ}$.

B.explanation: This is close to but smaller than the correct second-order value and does not follow from $\sin\theta = 2\lambda/d$ with the given numbers.

D.explanation: This is approximately twice $28.1^{\circ}$; angles cannot be doubled like this because $\theta = \sin^{-1}(n\lambda/d)$ is not linear in $n$.
